newsitem.title: USA: IMF, World Bank to launch debt relief for poor.
newsitem.headline: IMF, World Bank to launch debt relief for poor.

text.p: The IMF and World Bank are expected to put a long-awaited aid plan for poor nations into practice next week by approving debt relief for Uganda, international monetary sources said on Friday.

The move, which would come as the two lending agencies prepared for the start of their semi-annual meeting here, could eventually mean a reduction of hundreds of millions of dollars in the African nation's $3.4 billion of debt.
"I'm pretty sure that Uganda will get the go-ahead," said one source, who declined to be identified.

Uganda will be the first country to benefit from the multi-billion dollar debt relief plan that the International Monetary Fund and World Bank launched more than six months ago at their last semi-annual meeting here.
But sources said help for some other poor nations could be held up by political infighting among industrial countries over the scope of the programme.

The initiative, which combines the forces of the World Bank, the IMF and the Paris Cub of creditor nations, aims to reward poor countries that are carrying out tough economic reforms by providing them with debt relief. Up to about 25 countries, most in Africa, are expected to benefit from the plan, which could cost creditors as much as $7.7 billion.
Oxfam International, an umbrella group of 10 national aid agencies, criticised the IMF, the World Bank and some rich nations for delaying implementation of the initiative.

"The actions of those responsible for delaying debt reduction is resulting in lost opportunities for human development and -- in the last analysis, lost lives," it said in a report released this week.
Oxfam said even Uganda, which has a stellar 13-year record of economic reforms, is being short-changed by the plan because of a delay in when it will see its debts written off.

Under the initiative, most countries approved for debt relief would have to wait three years before receiving the full benefits of the programme. But nations with strong track records for reform could benefit sooner.

Bank and IMF staff have recommended that the waiting time be shortened to one year for Uganda. But the United States, mindful of the precedent that will be set for other countries, has argued for two years.

Oxfam criticised the U.S. stance, arguing that such a delay threatened the livelihoods of poor people. But a senior U.S. official, who declined to be named, said Washington was working to line up interim financing from the IMF and World Bank to ensure that Uganda does not suffer from an extended waiting period for debt relief.

The debt initiative has also run into political snags because of a drive by France to ensure that the Ivory Coast and some of its other African allies benefit from the programme. Under the current framework, the Ivory Coast would not be eligible because the level of its debt is not all that large when compared to its exports.

But France argues that penalises the country for having more open markets and says the initiative should also take into account the level of a country's debt in comparision to its government revenues from taxes and other sources.

Germany and Japan oppose changing the framework. As a compromise, the two sides have asked IMF and World Bank staff to try to come up with management guidelines for implementing the initiative that would allow countries like the Ivory Coast to participate without changing the framework.
